agent_responses.reasoning: The architecture as documented cannot be approved at this gate. The two most critical blockers are the absence of a timeout and the absence of a circuit breaker/fallback on a synchronous, blocking call to a third-party vendor sitting directly on the checkout critical path. These two gaps alone make it technically impossible to reliably meet the stated p99 latency acceptance criterion of 1.5s — any vendor slowness directly propagates to the customer. Additionally, the vendor's published SLA covers only availability at 99.5%, with no latency SLA documented, meaning we have no contractual basis for asserting the p99 target can be met. The single-point-of-failure risk and missing rollback plan compound the production risk. Before re-submission, the team must: (1) define and enforce a hard timeout on the vendor call well below 1.5s; (2) design a circuit breaker with an explicit fallback behavior (e.g., fail-open with risk flagging, async review queue, or secondary vendor); (3) obtain and document the vendor's p99 latency SLA; (4) produce a composite SLA calculation; and (5) document a rollback procedure.

agent_responses.reasoning: Both artifacts were read in full. The architecture describes a synchronous, blocking, critical-path call to a third-party AML screening vendor with no timeout, no circuit breaker, and no fallback — these are blocking defects given the stated p99 latency acceptance criterion and the total dependency on a 99.5%-SLA vendor. Beyond resilience, the architecture is silent on several security and privacy controls that are mandatory for a financial-crime screening integration: there is no audit logging of AML decisions (a likely regulatory requirement), no PCI scope assessment despite sitting on the checkout payment path, no documented cross-border data transfer mechanism for PII sent to a third party (GDPR exposure), and no log redaction controls for customer identity data. The combination of blocking operational risks and multiple unaddressed security/privacy gaps warrants a BLOCK at this gate. The team must resolve the timeout and circuit-breaker gaps, document and obtain a binding vendor SLA, establish audit logging, complete a PCI scope review, and produce a GDPR transfer impact assessment before re-submission.

concerns.concern_text: The AML screening vendor is documented with only a 99.5% uptime SLA, but there is no reference to a signed contract, formal SLA document, breach remedies, or financial penalties. Using an uncontracted third party on the critical checkout path creates unbounded legal and financial exposure.

The acceptance criterion requires checkout p99 latency under 1.5s, yet the vendor SLA is only 99.5% (up to ~3.6 hours downtime/month). A synchronous, blocking call to a 99.5%-SLA vendor mathematically prevents the checkout service from meeting any composite availability target above 99.5%, and latency spikes during vendor degradation will routinely breach the 1.5s p99 target.

The critical-path synchronous call to the AML vendor has no circuit breaker or fallback strategy defined. A slow or failed vendor response will cascade into checkout failures with no automatic mitigation, causing unbounded revenue loss.

No timeout is configured on the synchronous AML vendor call. Without a timeout, a hung vendor connection will block checkout threads indefinitely, risking thread-pool exhaustion and a full service outage. This also makes the 1.5s p99 latency acceptance criterion unenforceable.

No per-call cost ceiling, monthly spend cap, or usage-based budget alert is documented for the third-party AML screening vendor. Because calls are on the critical path for every checkout, unbounded transaction volume directly translates to unbounded vendor spend with no guardrail.

The architecture does not document whether the AML vendor is co-located, in the same cloud region, or cross-region/cross-cloud. If the synchronous call traverses regions, per-call egress costs at checkout volume could be material and are entirely unmodeled.

AML screening sits on the checkout critical path, which is typically co-mingled with cardholder data flows. No PCI scope assessment has been documented to confirm whether the AML vendor integration brings the vendor or any new network segment into PCI scope.

Customer identity and transaction data is transmitted to a third-party AML vendor. There is no documented legal transfer mechanism (e.g., SCCs, DPA, adequacy decision) to cover this data sharing, which may constitute a cross-border or controller-to-processor transfer under GDPR and similar regimes.

agent_responses.reasoning: This architecture has several blocking FinOps and legal issues that must be resolved before the gate can be approved. First, the third-party AML vendor lacks a documented SLA contract with breach remedies, creating legal exposure. Second, the synchronous blocking call has neither a timeout nor a circuit breaker, meaning any vendor degradation directly causes unbounded checkout outages and revenue loss. Third, the composite SLA math is broken: a 99.5% vendor SLA cannot support the stated p99 latency acceptance criterion on a blocking critical path. Fourth, there is no spend cap or egress cost model for per-call vendor charges at checkout volume. Fifth, PCI scope has not been assessed for the new data flow, and no legal transfer mechanism (DPA/SCCs) has been documented for transmitting customer data to the third party. All blocking-severity concerns must be remediated before this architecture can proceed.
